title: Why Do Ships Have a Bulb Under the Front?

scenes.text: When a giant ship sits in dry dock, you can see something strange below the waterline. At the very front, a huge rounded bulb sticks out, like the nose of a dolphin. You never see it when the ship is sailing. But it saves enormous amounts of fuel on every trip. Today, ten parts of a ship, and why each one exists.
scenes.caption: WHY THE BULB?

scenes.text: A big ship is one of the most efficient machines ever built. It can carry thousands of containers across an ocean, burning less fuel per tonne than a truck or a train. That efficiency comes from parts most people never see, many of them hidden under the water.
scenes.caption: HIDDEN UNDER THE WATER

scenes.text: As always, every fact here comes from a named source, maritime organisations, shipbuilders and naval references, all listed in the description. Let's start with the bulb.
scenes.caption: WHY DOES THIS EXIST?

scenes.text: Why do ships have a big bulb under the front? To fight waves. As a ship moves, it pushes water aside and creates a large wave at the bow. Making that wave costs energy, a lot of it. The bulb, sitting just below the surface, creates its own small wave, slightly ahead of the main one.
scenes.caption: WHY DOES THIS SHIP HAVE A BULB?
scenes.short: Why Do Ships Have a Bulb Under the Front?

scenes.text: If the bulb is shaped and placed correctly, its wave meets the main bow wave out of step, with a crest meeting a trough. The two partly cancel each other. The ship makes a smaller wave, and needs less power to move. On large ships at their design speed, the saving can be well over ten percent of the fuel.
scenes.caption: WAVES THAT CANCEL

scenes.text: There is a catch. The bulb works best at one speed and one depth in the water. When shipping companies started sailing slower to save fuel, some found that the old bulbs no longer helped, and even added drag. Some ships had their bows cut off and rebuilt with a new shape, just to match the new speed.
scenes.caption: ONE SPEED

scenes.text: Why are ship propellers so huge? Because a big, slow propeller is more efficient than a small, fast one. It pushes a large amount of water backwards, gently, rather than a small amount very fast. The propeller of a large container ship can be almost ten metres across and weigh over one hundred tonnes.
scenes.caption: WHY IS THIS PROPELLER SO HUGE?
scenes.short: Why Are Ship Propellers So Huge?

scenes.text: Spinning slowly also avoids a problem called cavitation. When a propeller blade spins too fast, the pressure on the back of the blade drops so low that the water boils into tiny bubbles, even in cold sea water. When those bubbles collapse, they hit the metal like tiny hammers, and they can eat holes in the blades.
scenes.caption: TINY HAMMERS

scenes.text: That is why giant propellers turn at around one hundred revolutions per minute, slower than a washing machine. Each one is cast in one piece from a bronze alloy and polished by hand. A small scratch or bend can cost fuel on every trip, for the life of the ship.
scenes.caption: SLOWER THAN A WASHING MACHINE

scenes.text: Why do many ships have a round tunnel going straight through the front of the hull? It holds a bow thruster, a propeller that pushes sideways. A big ship's main propeller and rudder only work well when the ship is moving forward. At very low speed, in a harbour, they cannot turn the front of the ship.
scenes.caption: WHY IS THERE A TUNNEL IN THE BOW?
scenes.short: Why Do Ships Have a Tunnel in the Bow?

scenes.text: The bow thruster solves that. By pushing water to the left or right, it swings the bow sideways, without the ship moving forward. Many ships have thrusters at the stern too. Together, they let a ship slide sideways into a berth, without needing tugboats every time.
scenes.caption: SIDEWAYS

scenes.text: The thruster tunnel is usually marked on the side of the hull with a sign, a circle with an arrow or the letters for thruster. It warns small boats and tugboats to stay clear, because the thruster can create a strong current that pulls or pushes them. A small sign for a powerful hidden part.
scenes.caption: STAY CLEAR

scenes.text: Why is there a circle with a line through it painted on the side of ships? It is the load line, also called the Plimsoll line. It shows how deep a ship can safely sit in the water. If the water rises above the line, the ship is overloaded, and it could sink in a storm.
scenes.caption: WHY IS THERE A CIRCLE ON THE SIDE?
scenes.short: Why Do Ships Have a Circle With a Line on the Side?

scenes.text: It is named after Samuel Plimsoll, a British politician who campaigned in the eighteen seventies against overloaded ships, which owners sometimes sent to sea knowing they might sink. The law made the mark mandatory. Next to the circle, a ladder of short lines shows different limits for different waters and seasons.
scenes.caption: SAMUEL PLIMSOLL

scenes.text: The ladder exists because water is not all the same. Fresh water is less dense than sea water, so a ship sinks deeper in a river. Cold water is denser than warm water. And winter seas are rougher, so ships must carry less. One painted mark keeps all these rules in one place.
scenes.caption: NOT ALL WATER IS THE SAME

scenes.text: Why is a ship's rudder placed right behind the propeller? Because the propeller blows a fast stream of water straight onto it. A rudder works by turning that flowing water, pushing the stern sideways. The faster the water, the stronger the push. Behind the propeller, the rudder gets the fastest water on the ship.
scenes.caption: WHY IS THE RUDDER BEHIND THE PROPELLER?
scenes.short: Why Is a Ship's Rudder Behind the Propeller?
scenes.file: File:Rudder and propeller Beached fishing vessel Nørre Vorupør Denmark 2017-04-14.jpg

scenes.text: This matters most at low speed. When the ship is moving slowly, the water around the hull is almost still, and a rudder in still water does nothing. But if the propeller is turning, it still blows water over the rudder, and the ship can steer. Captains use short bursts of power to turn in tight spaces.
scenes.caption: STEERING AT LOW SPEED

scenes.text: A large ship's rudder is the size of a house wall, and it is moved by powerful hydraulic machines. Even so, a giant ship turns slowly. It can take several kilometres to stop or make a full turn. That is why ships have to plan every move long before a harbour or a narrow channel.
scenes.caption: THE SIZE OF A WALL

scenes.text: Why do some ship propellers spin inside a ring? The ring is called a nozzle, or Kort nozzle, after the German engineer Ludwig Kort, who developed it. It is shaped like a short, thick tube, with a curved inside, like the cross section of a wing.
scenes.caption: WHY IS THIS PROPELLER INSIDE A RING?
scenes.short: Why Do Tugboat Propellers Spin Inside a Ring?
scenes.file: File:Union Sapphire close up of the propellor 11-Jan-2005.jpg

scenes.text: At low speed and high power, a propeller loses a lot of energy at the tips of its blades, where water slips around them. The ring stops that, and guides more water through the propeller. The ring itself is also shaped to produce extra thrust. Together, they can push much harder than an open propeller.
scenes.caption: MORE PUSH

scenes.text: That is why you see nozzles on tugboats, fishing trawlers and other ships that need to pull heavy loads at low speed. A tugboat is not built to go fast. It is built to push and pull a giant ship, and the nozzle gives it extra pulling power for its size.
scenes.caption: BUILT TO PULL

scenes.text: Why is the anchor chain more important than the anchor itself? Because most of the holding comes from the chain. A ship lets out much more chain than the depth of the water. The heavy chain lies along the sea floor, and it pulls on the anchor horizontally, so the anchor digs in instead of being lifted out.
scenes.caption: WHY IS THE CHAIN MORE IMPORTANT THAN THE ANCHOR?
scenes.short: Why Is the Anchor Chain More Important Than the Anchor?

scenes.text: The weight of the chain also acts like a spring. When a wave or the wind pulls the ship, the chain lifts off the seabed a little, absorbing the shock, and then settles back down. If the chain were short and straight, every pull would yank the anchor out of the sea floor.
scenes.caption: A HEAVY SPRING

scenes.text: A large ship's anchor chain is made of links that can weigh more than a hundred kilograms each. The chain runs into a locker deep inside the bow. When the anchor is dropped, it roars out in a cloud of rust and dust. One of the oldest tricks in shipping is still all about weight.
scenes.caption: IT'S ALL ABOUT WEIGHT

scenes.text: Why are there small metal blocks fixed to the hull of a ship? They are sacrificial anodes, usually made of zinc or aluminium. Steel in salt water rusts, through a slow electrical process. Two different metals in sea water act like a battery, and the more active metal corrodes first.
scenes.caption: WHY ARE THERE METAL BLOCKS ON THE HULL?
scenes.short: Why Do Ships Have Metal Blocks on the Hull?

scenes.text: Zinc and aluminium are more active than steel. So when they are attached to the hull, they corrode instead of the steel. They slowly dissolve, giving up their metal, while the hull stays protected. That is why they are called sacrificial. They die so the ship does not.
scenes.caption: THEY DIE SO THE SHIP DOESN'T

scenes.text: Anodes are placed near the propeller, the rudder and other parts where different metals meet, like the bronze propeller and the steel hull. They are checked and replaced in dry dock. A few cheap blocks of zinc protect a ship worth tens of millions.
scenes.caption: CHEAP BLOCKS, EXPENSIVE SHIP

scenes.text: Why does the bridge of a ship stick out past the sides of the hull? These extensions are called bridge wings. From the middle of the bridge, the officers cannot see the side of their own ship, or how close it is to the dock. From the end of a bridge wing, they can look straight down along the hull.
scenes.caption: WHY DOES THE BRIDGE STICK OUT TO THE SIDES?
scenes.short: Why Does a Ship's Bridge Stick Out to the Sides?

scenes.text: During docking, the captain and the pilot walk out onto the wing to see the gap between the ship and the quay. Many bridge wings have a small control station with the thrusters and engines, so the ship can be steered right from there. Some even have a glass floor to look straight down.
scenes.caption: LOOKING DOWN

scenes.text: On a giant container ship, the bridge can be hundreds of metres from the bow, and the view forward is partly blocked by containers. That is why the rules limit how much of the sea in front of the ship can be hidden. The bridge wings are the captain's eyes when the ship is closest to danger.
scenes.caption: THE CAPTAIN'S EYES

scenes.text: Why do oil tankers have two hulls, one inside the other? To stop oil spills. A single hull is only one layer of steel between the oil and the sea. If the ship hits a rock, the hull can tear open, and the oil flows straight out. With a double hull, there is a space between the outer skin and the tanks.
scenes.caption: WHY DOES THIS TANKER HAVE TWO HULLS?
scenes.short: Why Do Oil Tankers Have Two Hulls?

scenes.text: In nineteen eighty-nine, the tanker Exxon Valdez ran aground in Alaska and spilled a huge amount of crude oil, one of the worst environmental disasters of its time. After that, the United States passed laws requiring double hulls, and international rules soon followed for new tankers.
scenes.caption: AFTER EXXON VALDEZ

scenes.text: In a minor grounding, the outer hull can be damaged while the inner hull stays intact. The space between them can also hold ballast water when the ship is empty. A double hull does not make spills impossible, but it has made them much less common. Sometimes one disaster changes how every ship is built.
scenes.caption: ONE DISASTER CHANGED EVERY SHIP

scenes.text: So here are the ten. A bulb that cancels the bow wave. A giant slow propeller. A sideways thruster for docking. A painted line against overloading. A rudder in the propeller's stream. A ring that adds pulling power. A chain that holds more than the anchor. Blocks of zinc that sacrifice themselves. Bridge wings for the captain's eyes. And a double hull against oil spills.
scenes.caption: 10 PARTS. 10 REASONS.

scenes.text: The biggest machines on Earth hide their cleverest parts under the water. If you want more machines explained part by part, subscribe to Machine Reverse. And tell us in the comments which ship you want us to take apart next.
